Would a skyscraper hold together if a diagonal cut would be sawed through it in its entirety?
Depends on the angle of the cut. If it's shallow enough it might hold.

To expand on this: there are two main forces in play here.

First, there is gravity, that pulls the top segment down. Because the cut was made at an angle, some of the downforce is translated into sideways force that allows the top segment to slide sideways off the bottom segment. The lower you make the cut, the bigger the top segment will be, the bigger the downforce/sideways force will be.

Second, there is friction. Friction between the top segment and the bottom segment, where the cut is made. Friction depends almost entirely on the building material used.

The sideways force is counteracted by the friction force. If the sideways force overcomes the friction force, the top segment will slide off.

So it all depends on where you make the cut (high or low), the angle of the cut, and the building material used.

No. It would not.

Skyscrapers, any building over 40 stories (400 feet), under go significant structural loading from both gravity and wind. In the former, if you cut a building diagonally, then gravity will push the remaining structure down the incline plane you have created. That normal force is the resultant of two orthogonal vectors in the horizontal and vertical directions, meaning the component forces of that resultant will cause it to slide (hence the counteraction frictional force which will develop on the incline).

Wind loading on the structure tends to be taken as distributed along the face of the building causing horizontal translation and overturning about the structures center of gravity from uplift at the structure's base (necessitating embedded columns or columns bolted to the foundation). Typically wind-loading is considered to be uniformly distributed along the structure's face, however in reality the taller your building, the higher the wind-loading at the top, further contributing to uplift from overturning. Incidentally some buildings have deflections up to five feet or more in the horizontal direction from wind loads. Something which is inherent to the design of the structure and, to some extents, can be controlled for via things like the building's stiffness and other design choices.
